h1:
Bang Lang Dam Trip Plan
Boat, Raft & a Night on the Water
intro: Yala has a side a lot of people still don't know about: the lake above Bang Lang Dam, a sheet of emerald-green water ringed by the Hala-Bala forest. It's under an hour's drive from town, and once you're there you can hop on a boat, drift out on a raft, and fall asleep to the sound of water in the middle of the mountains. We've put this together as a 2-day, 1-night water trip so you can see exactly how to get there, where to board, what kind of raft to stay on and roughly what it costs — with a note on checking the situation before you go, since this is the deep-south border region.

blocks.html: Bang Lang Dam (some people call it Pattani Dam, since it holds back the Pattani River) sits in Bannang Sata district, Yala province. It's a clay-core rockfill dam, 85 metres high and 430 metres long, and the reservoir behind it spreads into a wide lake that runs all the way to the Hala-Bala forest. What makes this spot stand out is the still green water, the little islands poking up mid-lake, and the fact that there are real boat and raft services that take you into the forest.

We've laid this trip out as a 2-day, 1-night route, built around one night on a raft so you catch both the evening, when the sun drops behind the ridgeline, and the morning, when there's often a thin mist over the water. If you're short on time you can trim it to a single day there and back, but you'll miss the night out in the middle of the lake.

blocks.text: Before you go: check the situation and pack right

blocks.title: Read this before you set off
blocks.html: Yala is in the deep-south border region. The Bang Lang Dam–Betong route is one that travellers use regularly and people keep visiting, but before you actually head out you should check the latest news and safety announcements from local government agencies, and ask your accommodation or boat operator about conditions on the day you're going. You'll feel a lot more at ease. No need to panic — just have your information ready.

items: A private car is by far the easiest — there's no public transport that runs straight to the pier. If you don't have a car, rent one or arrange a private hire from Yala town.
Fill up in town — fuel stations around Bannang Sata and Than To are few and far between.
Bring cash — boat fares, raft fees and most waterfront food are cash-only, and the mobile signal is weak in places.
Call ahead to book a raft or boat, especially on long weekends, because the good rafts fill up fast.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Yala trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Yala
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.html: From Yala town, take Highway 410 (the Yala–Betong road) heading south. It's about 58 kilometres to the dam itself, roughly an hour's drive. Once you reach the Bannang Sata–Than To stretch, the road runs along the lake and the hillside, with pull-offs for lake photos here and there.

items: The dam crest and viewpoint above the reservoir — turn off Highway 410 toward the dam around the 46–47 km marker near Ban Kasod, then carry on about another 12 kilometres. You'll see the reservoir with the surrounding ridges.
Toh Ku Chae Bridge — a bridge across the lake on Highway 410 in the Mae Wat area, a wide-water viewpoint where people stop for photos on the way to Betong.
If you're carrying on to Betong, this same Highway 410 winds up into the hills all the way to Betong town.

blocks.text: 2 Days, 1 Night: the dam & lake route

blocks.html: Here's the plan we worked out to fit a drive from Yala town, one night on a raft, then more sightseeing the next morning before heading back. Times are rough — adjust them as you go.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Yala town → Bang Lang Dam → on the boat → overnight raft

items.activity: Leave Yala town, fill up and grab drinking water and snacks for the road
items.note: Get onto Highway 410, the Yala–Betong road

items.activity: Reach the Bang Lang Dam area, stop at the viewpoint above the reservoir and the dam crest for photos
items.note: Take in the reservoir before getting on the boat

items.activity: Head to the pier, arrange a boat or raft into Hala-Bala lake
items.note: Boat and raft services run roughly 09:00–18:00, and you can book ahead

items.activity: Cruise through the Hala-Bala forest, past Popcorn Island and the mid-lake islets
items.note: Still green water with mountains and forest behind — bring a hat and sunglasses

items.activity: Lunch on a raft or waterfront spot, fresh dam fish on the menu
items.note: Tilapia and red tilapia are what this area is known for

items.activity: Check in to your raft, swim and chill by the water — some rafts have a slide and inner tubes
items.note: Wear a life jacket every time you're in the water

items.activity: Watch the sun set behind the ridgeline from the raft
items.note: The best light of the day

items.activity: Dinner on the raft, then sleep to the sound of water in the middle of the lake
items.note: It's very quiet at night and the mobile signal can be weak

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Morning by the water → Than To Waterfall → home (or on to Betong)

items.activity: Wake up to morning on the water — there's often a thin mist drifting over the lake
items.note: Great for photos and a quiet coffee

items.activity: Breakfast on the raft, pack up and check out
Drive out and stop at Than To Waterfall in Bang Lang National Park
items.note: Several tiers, a short forest walk, and you can swim

items.activity: Lunch around Bannang Sata or Than To before deciding your route
Choose your way: back to Yala town, or on to Betong via Highway 410
items.note: The road to Betong is a winding climb — watch for fog and rain

blocks.text: Boats and rafts: which kind, and roughly what they cost

blocks.html: There are several water options at Bang Lang Dam, from a short scenic boat ride to chartering a whole raft for an overnight stay. The prices below are rough ranges from local operators — call the raft owner or pier to check before you actually go, since they shift with the season and the number of people.

items.name: Whole-raft charter, overnight (big group)
items.blurb: Rent the entire raft for a big group and stay overnight in the middle of the lake. There's bedding and breakfast, and some rafts come fully kitted out with a slide, inner tubes and life jackets. Great for coming as a group.
items.meta: 1 night · holds up to around 40 people per raft
items.price: from about ฿1,100 per group (basic) up to tens of thousands per raft (big rafts with a slide)

items.name: Round-trip boat cruise through Hala-Bala forest
items.blurb: A boat takes you out into the lake to see the Hala-Bala forest, Popcorn Island and the mid-lake islets, in the morning or afternoon. Good if you're short on time but still want the real views.
items.price: agree a charter price with the pier (depends on group size and distance)

items.name: Resort-style waterfront raft
items.blurb: Floating or waterfront accommodation set up as proper rooms, with a restaurant and café. The focus is on privacy and quiet — good for couples or a small family who don't want to share a big group raft.
items.price: varies by property, ask each one

blocks.title: Tips for picking a raft
blocks.html: If there are only a few of you but you still want to stay on a raft, ask about rafts that take you on a "shared" basis, or a raft resort — it works out better value than chartering a big raft to yourselves. And don't forget to ask whether there are enough life jackets for everyone before you commit to a booking.

items.name: Popcorn Island
items.blurb: A tiny freshwater island in the middle of the Bang Lang Dam lake, and a popular photo spot while you're cruising.

items.name: Than To Waterfall
items.blurb: A multi-tier waterfall in Bang Lang National Park, Tham Thalu subdistrict — a short forest walk, then a swim. A good stop on day two.

items.name: Toh Ku Chae Bridge
items.blurb: A bridge across the lake on Highway 410 in Mae Wat subdistrict, a wide-water viewpoint on the way to Betong.

blocks.text: What to eat around the dam

blocks.html: The standout food around the lake is fresh freshwater fish from the dam — both tilapia and red tilapia, done plenty of ways: fried, boiled, steamed or as larb. Lots of waterfront spots and rafts have it on the menu, with the price depending on the size of the fish, so ask before you order to avoid surprises.

items: Red tilapia / dam tilapia — the best of the area, fresh because it's raised in floating cages out on the water
Rice with southern curries and made-to-order dishes at shops in Bannang Sata and Than To districts
Keep some snacks and drinking water in the car for the stretches where shops are far apart

blocks.text: When's the best time to go

blocks.html: This side of the south gets heavy rain from late in the year into early the next (roughly November to January). The lake is at its best and the cruising is easiest after the rains have passed, when the air is clear and the water is still — and the thin morning mist over the water is exactly what a lot of people come for. If you go in the rainy season, build in a backup plan and check the weather and water level with the operator first.

blocks.title: Safety on the water
blocks.html: Wear a life jacket any time you're on a boat or in the water, keep a close eye on children, and don't force a trip out if the weather turns or the wind and waves pick up. Take your lead from what the boat driver and raft owner advise.

faq.q: How far is Bang Lang Dam from Yala town?
faq.a: About 58 kilometres via Highway 410, the Yala–Betong road — roughly an hour's drive. It's in Bannang Sata district. A private car is by far the easiest, since there's no public transport that runs straight to the pier.

faq.q: How much does an overnight raft at Bang Lang Dam cost?
faq.a: There are several levels, from a basic chartered raft starting around 1,100 THB per group, up to big rafts with a slide and full facilities running into the tens of thousands per raft. It's best to call and book with the raft owner in advance, especially over long weekends.

faq.q: Can you visit Bang Lang Dam in a single day?
faq.a: Yes. If you leave Yala town early, take a boat cruise through the Hala-Bala forest mid-morning, have dam fish for lunch and then head back. But staying one night on a raft adds the sunset and the morning mist over the lake.

faq.q: Is travelling around Yala and Bang Lang Dam safe?
faq.a: The Bang Lang Dam–Betong route is one that travellers use regularly and people keep visiting. But because it's in the deep-south border region, you should check the latest news and safety announcements from local agencies, and ask your accommodation or boat operator about conditions on the day you're going before you set off.

faq.q: When's the best time to cruise Bang Lang Dam?
faq.a: After the rains have passed, when the air is clear, the water is still and the views are sharp. Early morning in many seasons brings a beautiful thin mist over the water. Avoid the heavy rains from late in the year into early the next — or if you do go then, build in a backup plan and check the weather first.
